sentences.text: This ancient bird possessed broader wings than today's swifts and hindlimbs adapted for perching on tree branches.
The genus name Scaniacypselus combines the Latin name of the region where the type species was found with the old name Cypselus for the common swift.
The type species S. wardi possessed a short and stout humerus similar to that of modern swifts.
The ulna of S. wardi was relatively short and stout but more slender than in modern swifts.
S. szarskii had a relatively longer ulna and shorter carpometacarpus compared to modern swift relatives.
The tarsometatarsus of Scaniacypselus was highly reduced but more resembled that of treeswifts than modern swifts.
The feet of Scaniacypselus were anisodactyl, with three toes facing forward and one facing backward.
The tail feathers of Scaniacypselus were only lightly forked.
Many well-preserved specimens of Scaniacypselus with preserved plumage were found in the Messel Pit near Darmstadt, Germany.
Unlike highly aerial true swifts, Scaniacypselus lived a much less airborne life.
The first remains of Scaniacypselus were recovered by D.J. Ward from the Røsnæs Clay in Denmark.
The type species S. wardi is known only from a single, almost complete left wing specimen.
The species S. szarskii was originally described by Peters in 1985 as a species of Aegialornis from the Messel Pit in Germany.
Mayr and Peters transferred S. szarskii to the genus Scaniacypselus in 2001 based on an additional specimen.
Mayr classified Scaniacypselus as a basal member of the family Apodidae rather than the subfamily Apodinae.
Scaniacypselus lived during the Eocene epoch in Denmark, Germany, and France.
It is debated whether the incision on the sternum of Scaniacypselus has a specific function, as it appears inconsistently across specimens.
